translation: KJV — quoted exactly from the same source the Bible reader uses

people.name: Adam
people.identity: Formed from dust, in God's image
people.sceneCaption: In the garden of Eden — Genesis 2

ownWords.text: This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.

story: God formed him from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul (Genesis 2:7) — created in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), placed in Eden to dress it and to keep it, given every tree but one, and one command.

Alone among the creatures he had no counterpart, until God took from his side and made the woman — and Adam's first recorded words are a poem of recognition: 'This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh' (Genesis 2:23). And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.

Then came the serpent, the fruit, and the fall — and Adam's next recorded words are an excuse: 'The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat' (Genesis 3:12). The ground was cursed for his sake; yet even in judgment God clothed them with coats of skins (Genesis 3:21), and Adam named his wife Eve, mother of all living — holding the promise that her seed would bruise the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15, 20).

verses.text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.
And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.

people.name: Eve
people.sceneCaption: The tree in the midst of the garden — Genesis 3

ownWords.text: I have gotten a man from the Lord.

story: She was taken from Adam's side while he slept — 'And the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man' (Genesis 2:22) — the crown of the creation, a help meet for him, bearing with him the image of God.

The serpent came to her first, questioning the one command — and she took of the fruit, and gave also unto her husband with her, and he did eat. Questioned by God, her recorded words are honest and short: 'The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat' (Genesis 3:13).

Judgment fell — and inside it, a promise aimed past her to her seed, who would bruise the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15): the first gospel, spoken over the first sinners. Adam named her Eve, because she was the mother of all living (Genesis 3:20); and her own voice rings with hope at her firstborn's birth: 'I have gotten a man from the Lord' (Genesis 4:1).

verses.text: And the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.
And the Lord God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.
And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
And Adam called his wife’s name Eve; because she was the mother of all living.

people.name: Noah
people.sceneCaption: The bow in the cloud — Genesis 9

ownWords.text: Blessed be the Lord God of Shem; and Canaan shall be his servant.

hallLine.text: By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith:

story: In a generation where the wickedness of man was great and every imagination of his heart was only evil continually, one man stood out: 'But Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord' — 'a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God' (Genesis 6:8–9).

Warned of a flood no eye had ever seen, he believed the warning and built — 'By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house' (Hebrews 11:7). The record's verdict on that enormous obedience is one line: 'Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he' (Genesis 6:22).

Through the flood and out the other side, Noah built an altar, and God set His bow in the cloud as the token of His covenant with every living creature (Genesis 9:13). His recorded words bless the line of Shem — 'Blessed be the Lord God of Shem' (Genesis 9:26) — the line through which the promise would travel; and of his three sons was the whole earth overspread (Genesis 9:19).

verses.text: But Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord.
These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God.
Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he.

people.name: Jacob
people.identity: The wrestler who would not let go

ownWords.text: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.

hallLine.text: By faith Jacob, when he was a dying, blessed both the sons of Joseph; and worshipped, leaning upon the top of his staff.

story: The younger twin who grasped his brother's heel, bought the birthright for a meal, and took the blessing in disguise — Jacob ran from home with a staff and a promise he had not yet made his own. At Bethel he dreamed of a ladder set up on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and woke in awe: 'Surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not... this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven' (Genesis 28:16–17).

Twenty years of exile followed — wives, children, flocks — and on the way home, facing the brother he had wronged, Jacob was left alone at the ford Jabbok, 'and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day' (Genesis 32:24). Wounded in the hollow of his thigh, he still would not release his grip: 'I will not let thee go, except thou bless me' (Genesis 32:26).

He came away with a new name — 'Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed' (Genesis 32:28) — and a limp he carried the rest of his life. The twelve tribes bear his sons' names; and Hebrews remembers his end in worship, blessing Joseph's sons, leaning upon the top of his staff (Hebrews 11:21).

verses.text: And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not.
And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.
And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.

people.name: Abraham
people.sceneCaption: The promise counted in stars — Genesis 15

hallLine.text: By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.

story: Abraham — first called Abram — was living in Haran when God called him to leave his country and his father's house for a land he had never seen, with a promise: a great nation, a great name, and blessing for all families of the earth through him (Genesis 12). He went, not knowing where he was going.

Childless into old age, he was brought outside under the night sky and told his descendants would be as the stars — and he believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness (Genesis 15). Isaac, the son of promise, was born to him and Sarah in their old age.

When God tested him on Mount Moriah, Abraham offered Isaac — and was stayed at the final moment, accounting that God was able to raise him up (Genesis 22; Hebrews 11:17–19). Every promise the rest of the story stands on runs through this man's obedience. He is called the friend of God, and the father of all who believe.

verses.text: By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.
By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered up Isaac: and he that had received the promises offered up his only begotten son,

people.versesPending: Genesis 15:6 and his own words (Genesis 22:8) — sourcing pass owed

people.name: Joseph

hallLine.text: By faith Joseph, when he died, made mention of the departing of the children of Israel; and gave commandment concerning his bones.

story: Joseph was Jacob's beloved son, given a coat of many colours — and hated by his brothers for it, and for his dreams. They sold him to traders bound for Egypt, and told their father he was dead (Genesis 37).

In Egypt he rose in Potiphar's house, was falsely accused, and was forgotten in prison — until Pharaoh's dreams brought him out. Joseph interpreted them: seven years of plenty, seven of famine. Pharaoh set him over all Egypt, second only to the throne (Genesis 41).

When the famine drove his brothers down to Egypt for grain, Joseph tested them, then wept and revealed himself: “I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt.” He brought his whole family down and kept them alive. At the end he spoke the line his whole life proves: what his brothers meant for evil, God meant for good (Genesis 50:20). Dying, he spoke of the exodus still to come and made them swear to carry his bones up (Genesis 50:24–25).

verses.text: By faith Joseph, when he died, made mention of the departing of the children of Israel; and gave commandment concerning his bones.

people.versesPending: Genesis 50:20 (his own words) — sourcing pass owed

people.name: Moses
people.sceneCaption: Through the sea on dry ground — Exodus 14

ownWords.text: Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh, and that I should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt?

hallLine.text: By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;

story: Moses was born in Egypt under Pharaoh's command that Hebrew sons be killed, hidden by his mother, and drawn out of the Nile by Pharaoh's own daughter (Exodus 2). Raised in the palace, he fled to Midian after killing an Egyptian overseer, and spent forty years keeping sheep.

At the burning bush on Horeb, God called him by name and sent him back to Egypt: “I AM hath sent me unto you” (Exodus 3:14). Through the plagues, the Passover, and the Red Sea — where Israel passed through on dry ground — Moses led a nation of slaves out of the house of bondage (Exodus 12–14).

On Sinai he received the Law; for forty years he bore a stubborn people through the wilderness, interceding for them again and again. He died on Mount Nebo, within sight of the land he had led them to (Deuteronomy 34). Hebrews remembers him as the man who esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt.

verses.text: And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
By faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king: for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.
By faith they passed through the Red sea as by dry land: which the Egyptians assaying to do were drowned.

people.name: Gideon
people.identity: The least of his father's house

ownWords.text: Oh my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel? behold, my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.

hallLine.text: And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:

story: Israel had done evil in the sight of the LORD, and for seven years the Midianites swept the land at harvest, leaving no sustenance for Israel — the people hid in dens, caves and strongholds (Judges 6:1–6). In that fear, Gideon son of Joash threshed wheat by a winepress, hiding it from the raiders, when the angel of the LORD sat under an oak at Ophrah and greeted him: "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour" (Judges 6:11–12).

Gideon's answer was an honest protest — if the LORD is with us, why is all this befallen us? — and when the call came ("Go in this thy might... have not I sent thee?"), he named his weakness plainly: "my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house" (Judges 6:13–15). That night he threw down his father's altar of Baal and built an altar to the LORD, doing it by night because he feared the men of the city (Judges 6:25–27). When the Spirit of the LORD came upon him and he blew the trumpet, he still asked for a sign — twice — with a fleece of wool, and God answered both times (Judges 6:34–40).

Then God shrank the army instead of growing it: twenty-two thousand went home, and at the water only three hundred remained — "lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me" (Judges 7:2–7). In the middle watch, three companies with trumpets, empty pitchers and lamps inside the pitchers cried, "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon," and the LORD set every man's sword against his fellow throughout the host (Judges 7:16–22). Hebrews counts the least of his father's house among those who "out of weakness were made strong" (Hebrews 11:32–34).

verses.text: And the angel of the Lord appeared unto him, and said unto him, The Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour.
And he said unto him, Oh my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel? behold, my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.
But the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon, and he blew a trumpet; and Abi–ezer was gathered after him.
And the Lord said unto Gideon, By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you, and deliver the Midianites into thine hand: and let all the other people go every man unto his place.

people.name: Boaz
people.sceneCaption: At the gate of Bethlehem — Ruth 4

ownWords.text: The Lord recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the Lord God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.

story: Boaz enters the record as a mighty man of wealth, of the family of Elimelech, in Bethlehem (Ruth 2:1). When the widowed Moabite Ruth came to glean behind his reapers, he protected her: he charged his young men not to touch her, gave her water from the vessels and bread and parched corn at mealtime, and commanded handfuls of grain to be let fall on purpose for her to gather (Ruth 2:8–16).

His blessing over her shows the man. He had heard all she had done for her mother-in-law since her husband's death — how she had left her father and her mother and the land of her nativity, and come to a people she had not known before (Ruth 2:11). "The LORD recompense thy work," he told her, "and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust" (Ruth 2:12).

As near kinsman, Boaz settled the redemption in the open, at the gate of the city, before ten men of the elders. When the nearer kinsman declined — lest he mar his own inheritance — Boaz bought all that was Elimelech's and took Ruth to be his wife, "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance" (Ruth 4:1–10). Their son Obed became the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:17, 22), and Matthew's genealogy carries Boaz by name in the line of the Messiah: "Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth" (Matthew 1:5).

verses.text: And Boaz answered and said unto her, It hath fully been shewed me, all that thou hast done unto thy mother in law since the death of thine husband: and how thou hast left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity, and art come unto a people which thou knewest not heretofore.
The Lord recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the Lord God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.

Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren, and from the gate of his place: ye are witnesses this day.

people.name: Samson

ownWords.text: O Lord God, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes.

hallLine.text: And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:

story: Samson was promised before he was born. To Manoah's barren wife the angel of the LORD announced a son who would be a Nazarite unto God from the womb — no razor should come on his head — and who would begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines (Judges 13:3–5). The child grew, and the LORD blessed him; and the Spirit of the LORD began to move him at times in the camp of Dan (Judges 13:24–25).

His strength made him the terror of the Philistines — but Samson loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah, and the lords of the Philistines bought her betrayal at eleven hundred pieces of silver each. She pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death, until he told her all his heart (Judges 16:4–17). Shorn in his sleep, he woke and said, "I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself. And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him" (Judges 16:20). The Philistines took him, put out his eyes, bound him with fetters of brass, and he did grind in the prison house (Judges 16:21).

But the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven (Judges 16:22). Brought out to make sport for the Philistines in the house of Dagon, the blind strongman asked the lad who held his hand to let him feel the pillars whereupon the house stood — and prayed his last prayer: "O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God" (Judges 16:26–28). He bowed himself with all his might, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people therein; "so the dead which he slew at his death were more than they which he slew in his life" (Judges 16:30). Hebrews still counts Samson by name among the faithful (Hebrews 11:32).

verses.text: And Samson called unto the Lord, and said, O Lord God, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes.

And Samson said, Let me die with the Philistines. And he bowed himself with all his might; and the house fell upon the lords, and upon all the people that were therein. So the dead which he slew at his death were more than they which he slew in his life.

people.name: Rizpah
people.identity: The mother who kept the watch
story: Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, was a concubine of King Saul. Years after Saul's death a famine held the land three years, year after year, and David enquired of the LORD. The answer named the cause: "It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites" (2 Samuel 21:1). To make the atonement the Gibeonites asked for seven men of Saul's sons — and the king took the two sons of Rizpah, Armoni and Mephibosheth, among them (2 Samuel 21:5–8).

The seven were hanged in the hill before the LORD, in the first days of barley harvest (2 Samuel 21:9). Rizpah could not save her sons, but she would not leave them. She took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night (2 Samuel 21:10). Through the whole harvest, one mother kept the watch alone.

And it was told David what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done (2 Samuel 21:11). Her vigil moved the king: David took the bones of Saul and of Jonathan and gathered the bones of them that were hanged, and buried them in the sepulchre of Kish in the country of Benjamin — and after that God was intreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:12–14). Scripture records no words of Rizpah. Her sackcloth on the rock is her speech, and it reached the king.

verses.text: But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite:

And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.
And it was told David what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done.

people.name: Elijah

ownWords.text: Hear me, O Lord, hear me, that this people may know that thou art the Lord God, and that thou hast turned their heart back again.

story: In the third year, with a sore famine in Samaria, the word of the LORD sent Elijah to shew himself unto Ahab (1 Kings 18:1–2). Ahab met him with an accusation — "Art thou he that troubleth Israel?" — and Elijah threw it back: the trouble was Ahab's, who had forsaken the commandments of the LORD and followed Baalim. Then he summoned all Israel to mount Carmel, and the prophets of Baal four hundred and fifty with them (1 Kings 18:17–20).

On the mountain he put the question the whole nation was dodging: "How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word" (1 Kings 18:21). Baal's prophets took their bullock and cried on their god from morning until noon, and leaped upon the altar, and cut themselves — but there was neither voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded (1 Kings 18:25–29). Elijah repaired the altar of the LORD that was broken down, built it of twelve stones, and had the sacrifice drenched with water three times, until the trench around the altar was full (1 Kings 18:30–35).

Then, at the time of the evening sacrifice, the prophet prayed two short verses: "LORD God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel... Hear me, O LORD, hear me, that this people may know that thou art the LORD God" (1 Kings 18:36–37). And the fire of the LORD fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench — and all the people fell on their faces and said, "The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God" (1 Kings 18:38–39). Before the day ended, Elijah was on Carmel again with his face between his knees, sending his servant seven times toward the sea, until a little cloud like a man's hand rose — and the heaven was black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain (1 Kings 18:42–45).

verses.text: And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
Hear me, O Lord, hear me, that this people may know that thou art the Lord God, and that thou hast turned their heart back again.
And when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces: and they said, The Lord, he is the God; the Lord, he is the God.

people.name: Elisha
people.sceneCaption: The mantle and the Jordan — 2 Kings 2

ownWords.text: I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me.

story: When the LORD would take up Elijah into heaven by a whirlwind, Elisha would not be left behind. At Beth–el and again at Jericho the sons of the prophets told him that his master would be taken from his head that day — and three times over he answered the same vow: "As the LORD liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee" (2 Kings 2:1–6). They two stood by Jordan, and Elijah wrapped his mantle together and smote the waters, and they went over on dry ground (2 Kings 2:7–8).

On the far side, Elijah asked what he should do for him before he was taken. Elisha asked for the firstborn's share of the inheritance: "I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me" (2 Kings 2:9). As they still went on and talked, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven (2 Kings 2:11). Elisha cried, "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof" — then took up the mantle that fell from him, stood by the bank of Jordan, smote the waters and said, "Where is the LORD God of Elijah?" and the waters parted for him also (2 Kings 2:12–14).

The double portion showed itself in how he saw the world. At Dothan, with the Syrian host compassing the city by night, his servant cried, "Alas, my master! how shall we do?" Elisha answered, "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them" — and prayed, "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see." The young man's eyes were opened, and the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha (2 Kings 6:15–17).

verses.text: And it came to pass, when they were gone over, that Elijah said unto Elisha, Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee. And Elisha said, I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me.

And he took the mantle of Elijah that fell from him, and smote the waters, and said, Where is the Lord God of Elijah? and when he also had smitten the waters, they parted hither and thither: and Elisha went over.
And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.

And Elisha prayed, and said, Lord, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the Lord opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha.

people.name: Isaiah
people.identity: The prophet who saw the King

ownWords.text: Here am I; send me.

story: In the year that King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, His train filling the temple, seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy' until the posts of the door moved (Isaiah 6:1–4). The vision first undid him — 'Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips' (Isaiah 6:5) — then a seraph touched his mouth with a live coal from the altar, and his sin was purged.

Cleansed, he heard the question that has echoed through every calling since: 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' His answer is the shortest commission in Scripture: 'Here am I; send me' (Isaiah 6:8). He was sent to a people who would hear and not understand — and he went anyway, prophesying through the reigns of kings for a lifetime.

From Isaiah's scroll shines the clearest sight of Jesus in all the Old Testament: the child whose name shall be called 'Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace' (Isaiah 9:6) — and the suffering servant, 'wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities... and with his stripes we are healed' (Isaiah 53:5). Seven centuries early, he saw Him whole.

verses.text: Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts.
Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.

people.name: Ruth
people.identity: The loyalty that entered the line
people.sceneCaption: Gleaning in the fields of Boaz — Ruth 2

ownWords.text: Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:

story: Ruth was a Moabite woman married into a Bethlehem family that had fled a famine. When her husband, his brother, and his father all died in Moab, her mother-in-law Naomi set out for home — and Ruth refused to be sent back. Her vow to Naomi is one of the great speeches of the Old Testament: “whither thou goest, I will go… thy God my God” (Ruth 1:16–17).

In Bethlehem she gleaned in the fields to feed them both, working behind the reapers in the field of Boaz, a kinsman of Naomi's family, who showed her favour and protection (Ruth 2). Following Naomi's counsel, Ruth came to Boaz at the threshing floor, and he — as kinsman-redeemer — married her (Ruth 3–4).

Her son Obed became the grandfather of King David (Ruth 4:17, 22). The Moabite widow who chose Israel's God stands in the direct line of the Messiah: Matthew's genealogy names her — “Booz begat Obed of Ruth” (Matthew 1:5).

verses.text: And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the Lord do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me.

people.name: King Saul
people.identity: The first king, who lost the kingdom

ownWords.text: And Saul said unto Samuel, I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.

story: Israel asked for a king to rule them like the nations, and the man God gave them was Saul the son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin — head and shoulders taller than any man in Israel, with none goodlier among the people (1 Samuel 9:1–2). Samuel anointed him with oil in private, then presented him to the tribes at Mizpeh; when the lot fell on Saul he was found hidden among the baggage, and the people shouted, 'God save the king' (1 Samuel 10:17–24). His reign opened in victory: he mustered Israel and broke the Ammonite siege of Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11).

The cracks came early, and they were cracks of obedience. At Gilgal, with his army scattering, Saul forced himself and offered the burnt offering that was Samuel's to give (1 Samuel 13). Sent against Amalek with a plain command to destroy all, he spared King Agag and the best of the flocks — and blamed the people when Samuel confronted him (1 Samuel 15). Samuel's sentence over Saul's reign has never been improved: 'to obey is better than sacrifice' — and the kingdom was torn from Saul that day, and given to a neighbour better than he (1 Samuel 15:22, 28).

Twice Saul said the words — 'I have sinned' (1 Samuel 15:24, 30) — yet in the same breath he asked Samuel to honour him before the elders of the people, and the crown still passed to David, the shepherd Samuel anointed in Bethlehem. Saul spent his last years hunting the man he knew would replace him, while David spared his life twice. He died on Mount Gilboa, fallen on his own sword in the Philistine rout (1 Samuel 31) — and Paul keeps his place in the story exact: God gave Israel Saul, 'and when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David' (Acts 13:21–22).

verses.text: And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people.
And Samuel said to all the people, See ye him whom the Lord hath chosen, that there is none like him among all the people? And all the people shouted, and said, God save the king.
And Saul said unto Samuel, I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.
Then he said, I have sinned: yet honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord thy God.

people.name: David
people.sceneCaption: One stone in the valley of Elah — 1 Samuel 17

ownWords.text: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.

story: David was the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, keeping his father's sheep, when the prophet Samuel anointed him king in place of Saul (1 Samuel 16). Sent to the battle lines with food for his brothers, he heard Goliath of Gath defying Israel — and went down into the valley of Elah with a staff, a sling, and five smooth stones. The giant fell, and Israel's army routed the Philistines (1 Samuel 17).

Hunted by Saul for years, David spared the king's life twice, and at Saul's death was crowned — first over Judah, then over all Israel. He took Jerusalem, brought up the ark, and received God's promise that his house and kingdom would be established for ever (2 Samuel 7).

He was also the psalmist: the shepherd's songs — “The Lord is my shepherd” (Psalm 23) — are his. Scripture does not hide his fall with Bathsheba or his repentance (Psalm 51). The Messiah is promised as the Son of David, and Matthew's gospel opens with his name: “Jesus Christ, the son of David” (Matthew 1:1).

verses.text: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.

people.versesPending: 1 Samuel 17:45 (his words to Goliath) — sourcing pass owed

people.name: Esther
people.identity: For such a time as this
story: Esther — Hadassah — was a Jewish orphan in Susa, raised by her cousin Mordecai, in the days of King Ahasuerus of Persia. When the king sought a new queen, Esther was taken into the palace and chosen above all the women (Esther 2). Mordecai charged her not to reveal her people.

When Haman, the king's chief officer, plotted to destroy all the Jews of the empire on a day fixed by lot, Mordecai sent word to Esther: she must go before the king — though approaching him unsummoned meant death unless he held out the golden sceptre. After three days of fasting, she went in. The king held out the sceptre (Esther 5).

Across two banquets she exposed Haman's plot to the king. Haman was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai, and the king's new decree let the Jews defend themselves; the days appointed for their destruction became the feast of Purim (Esther 7–9).

verses.text: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
Then Esther bade them return Mordecai this answer,

Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.
Then Esther the queen answered and said, If I have found favour in thy sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request:

people.name: Daniel
people.sceneCaption: The mouths of lions, stopped — Daniel 6
story: Daniel was carried to Babylon as a young man when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, and was chosen for the king's court. There he purposed in his heart not to defile himself with the king's food, and God gave him favour and wisdom above all the king's counsellors (Daniel 1).

He interpreted Nebuchadnezzar's dream when every wise man of Babylon had failed, read the handwriting on the wall for Belshazzar on the night Babylon fell, and served under Darius the Mede (Daniel 2; 5; 6).

When a decree forbade prayer to any but the king, Daniel opened his windows toward Jerusalem and prayed three times a day, as before. He was cast into the den of lions — and found unhurt in the morning, because he believed in his God (Daniel 6:22–23). His visions reach to the end of the age: kingdoms rising and falling, and one like the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven (Daniel 7:13).

verses.text: Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions,

people.name: John the Baptist

ownWords.text: He must increase, but I must decrease.

story: John was born to Zechariah and Elizabeth in their old age, announced by Gabriel as the one who would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1). He came preaching in the wilderness of Judaea — “Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” — clothed in camel's hair, baptizing in the Jordan all who confessed their sins (Matthew 3).

When Jesus came to be baptized, John pointed his own disciples to him: “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). Jesus said of him that among those born of women none had risen greater (Matthew 11:11).

John rebuked Herod for his unlawful marriage and was imprisoned, and in prison sent to ask Jesus, “Art thou he that should come?” Jesus answered by pointing to the works themselves (Matthew 11:2–5). Herod later had him beheaded at Herodias's request (Matthew 14). His whole ministry is in his own sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

verses.text: He must increase, but I must decrease.
Verily I say unto you, Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.

people.name: Mary
story: Mary was a young woman of Nazareth, betrothed to Joseph, when the angel Gabriel came to her with an announcement no one had ever heard: she would conceive and bear a son, Jesus, who would be called the Son of the Highest, and of his kingdom there would be no end (Luke 1:26–33). Her answer was surrender: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word” (Luke 1:38). Her song — the Magnificat — pours out of her visit to Elizabeth (Luke 1:46–55).

She bore Jesus in Bethlehem, laid him in a manger, received shepherds and wise men, and kept all these things and pondered them in her heart (Luke 2). She raised him in Nazareth, was there at Cana when his first sign turned water into wine (John 2), and stood by the cross when he died, where he gave her into the care of the beloved disciple (John 19:25–27).

After the resurrection she is found with the apostles in the upper room, continuing in prayer (Acts 1:14). She stands in the Scarlet Thread: through Mary, of the house of David, the promise reached its destination.

verses.text: And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her.
But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.
His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.

people.name: Mary Magdalene

ownWords.text: Rabboni

story: She first appears in the record among the women who followed Jesus from Galilee and ministered unto Him — 'Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils' (Luke 8:2). Whatever had held her, He had cast it out; and from then on she is never far from Him — standing by the cross when most had fled, watching where He was laid.

On the first day of the week she came to the sepulchre early, when it was yet dark, and found the stone taken away (John 20:1). She ran for Peter and John — but when they went home, she stayed: weeping at the tomb, questioning the angels, pleading with a man she supposed to be the gardener to tell her where they had laid Him, that she might take Him away.

Then He spoke her name — 'Mary' — and she turned and answered with one word: 'Rabboni; which is to say, Master' (John 20:16). The risen Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene (Mark 16:9), and He sent her as the first messenger of the resurrection: 'Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had spoken these things unto her' (John 20:18).

verses.text: And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils,
Now when Jesus was risen early the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, out of whom he had cast seven devils.
Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master.
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had spoken these things unto her.

people.name: Jesus
people.identity: The centre of the whole story
people.sceneCaption: The empty tomb at dawn — John 20

ownWords.text: I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.

story: Jesus was born in Bethlehem to Mary, of the line of David, and raised in Nazareth. At about thirty he was baptized by John in the Jordan, and began preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God through Galilee and Judaea — teaching in parables, healing the sick, raising the dead, and gathering twelve apostles (Matthew 4; Mark 1).

He told his disciples plainly who he was and what was coming: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6); “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Betrayed by Judas, he was tried before the Sanhedrin and Pontius Pilate and crucified in Jerusalem — and on the third day the tomb was found empty, and he appeared to his disciples alive (John 20; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8).

Every person in this hall stands in relation to him: the patriarchs believed the promise of him, the prophets spoke of him, John pointed to him, and the apostles went to the world with him. He is not one witness among many. He is the centre the river runs to.

verses.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

people.name: Peter
story: Peter — Simon, son of Jonah — was a fisherman of Galilee when Jesus called him from his nets: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19). He was first among the twelve in every list, quick to speak and quick to act: he stepped out of the boat to walk on the sea toward Jesus, and began to sink when he saw the wind (Matthew 14:28–31).

At Caesarea Philippi he made the confession the church is built on: “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God” — and Jesus answered, “upon this rock I will build my church” (Matthew 16:16–18). In the night of the trial he denied Jesus three times, as Jesus had said; after the resurrection, by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus restored him three times: “Feed my sheep” (John 21).

At Pentecost it was Peter who stood up and preached, and about three thousand were added that day (Acts 2). He opened the door of the gospel to the Gentiles at Cornelius's house (Acts 10), and his two letters still close the New Testament's witness: written, tradition holds, from Rome, where he died under Nero.

verses.text: And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.
And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Bar–jona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

people.name: Paul
people.sceneCaption: The light on the Damascus road — Acts 9
story: Paul — first Saul of Tarsus — was a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, and a persecutor of the church: he held the coats of those who stoned Stephen, and was on his way to Damascus with authority to bind Christians when a light from heaven struck him down and the risen Jesus spoke to him: “Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” (Acts 7:58; 9:1–5).

Blinded, then baptized by Ananias, he became the apostle to the Gentiles. Across three missionary journeys he planted churches through Cyprus, Galatia, Macedonia, Greece and Asia, preaching in synagogues and marketplaces, working as a tentmaker, enduring shipwreck, beatings, stonings and prison (Acts 13–28; 2 Corinthians 11).

His letters — Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians and the rest — make up much of the New Testament. Arrested in Jerusalem, he appealed to Caesar and was carried to Rome, where Acts leaves him preaching the kingdom with all confidence, no man forbidding him (Acts 28:31).

verses.text: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

people.name: Andrew
people.identity: The first to follow, who brought others

ownWords.text: He first findeth his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ.

story: Andrew was a disciple of John the Baptist before he was a disciple of Jesus. Standing by the Jordan, he heard John point at Jesus — 'Behold the Lamb of God' — and followed, and stayed with Jesus that day (John 1:35–40). The first thing the record shows him doing is the thing he always does: 'He first findeth his own brother Simon Peter, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias... And he brought him to Jesus' (John 1:41–42).

It is Andrew again at the feeding of the five thousand — the one who finds the lad with five barley loaves and two small fishes, and names the gap honestly: 'but what are they among so many?' (John 6:8–9). Jesus took what Andrew found and fed the multitude with it. And when Greeks came up to the feast asking to see Jesus, they came to Philip, Philip came to Andrew, and Andrew and Philip together told Jesus (John 12:20–22).

The Gospels give Andrew no miracles and no sermons; his gift is introductions — a brother, a boy with a lunch, strangers from Greece. He stands in every list of the twelve (Matthew 10:2), and after the ascension he is there in the upper room, continuing in prayer with the rest (Acts 1:13–14). The first man to follow Jesus is remembered, fittingly, for the people he brought with him.

verses.text: He first findeth his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ.
One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, saith unto him,
There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?
Philip cometh and telleth Andrew: and again Andrew and Philip tell Jesus.

people.name: James son of Zebedee
people.identity: A son of thunder, first of the twelve to fall
people.sceneCaption: Mending nets by the sea — Matthew 4

ownWords.text: They said unto him, Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory.

story: James was in the boat with his father Zebedee and his brother John, mending their nets, when Jesus came along the shore of Galilee and called them: 'And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them. And immediately they left the ship and their father, and followed him' (Matthew 4:21–22).

With Peter and John, James was taken closest in: present when Jesus raised Jairus's daughter, on the mountain when he was transfigured, and near him in Gethsemane (Mark 5:37; 9:2; 14:33). Jesus surnamed the brothers Boanerges — 'the sons of thunder' (Mark 3:17) — and the thunder shows: they asked to call fire down on a Samaritan village that would not receive Jesus (Luke 9:54), and they came asking for the thrones at his right and left hand in his glory (Mark 10:37). Jesus answered with a cup and a baptism they did not yet understand — and of the two brothers, James drank of that cup first.

After Pentecost, when Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex the church, 'he killed James the brother of John with the sword' (Acts 12:2). James is the first of the twelve to die for the name of Jesus — the only one of the twelve whose martyrdom Scripture itself records. The son of thunder who asked for a seat in glory received instead the martyr's crown, first of the twelve to wear it.

verses.text: And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them.
And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him.
They said unto him, Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory.
And he killed James the brother of John with the sword.

people.name: John the Apostle
people.sceneCaption: At the foot of the cross — John 19
story: John was the younger of Zebedee's sons, called with James from the nets (Matthew 4:21–22) and taken, with Peter and James, closer than the rest — into Jairus's house, up the mountain of transfiguration, and a little farther into Gethsemane (Mark 5:37; 9:2; 14:33). In his own Gospel he never writes his name. He is 'the disciple whom Jesus loved' (John 13:23; 21:20) — the one who leaned on Jesus' breast at the last supper and asked who the betrayer would be (John 13:23–25).

Of the twelve, John alone is placed at the cross: 'When Jesus therefore saw his mother, and the disciple standing by, whom he loved, he saith unto his mother, Woman, behold thy son! Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home' (John 19:26–27). On the resurrection morning he outran Peter to the sepulchre, stooped down, saw the linen clothes lying — 'and believed' (John 20:2–8).

His Gospel signs itself: 'This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true' (John 21:24). Three letters carry his name, and the last book of the Bible came to him in exile — 'I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation... was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ' (Revelation 1:9). The son of thunder became the apostle of love: 'God is love' is his summary of the whole matter (1 John 4:8).

verses.text: When Jesus therefore saw his mother, and the disciple standing by, whom he loved, he saith unto his mother, Woman, behold thy son!
Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home.
This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true.

I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ, was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ.

people.name: Philip
people.identity: The one who said, Come and see

ownWords.text: Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.

story: Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44). The day after Andrew first followed Jesus, 'Jesus... findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me' (John 1:43). Philip's first recorded act is Andrew's act — he went and found someone: 'Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph' (John 1:45).

Philip is the apostle Jesus tested with a sum. Seeing the great crowd coming, Jesus asked him where bread could be bought to feed them — 'and this he said to prove him: for he himself knew what he would do' (John 6:5–6). Philip answered from the ledger: 'Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little' (John 6:7). The feeding, when it came, did not come out of Philip's arithmetic; it came from a boy's loaves in Jesus' hands.

At the last supper Philip made the request the whole church has prayed since: 'Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us' (John 14:8). The answer stands among the greatest sentences in the Gospel: 'Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father' (John 14:9). Philip is named among the apostles waiting in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13). (The Philip of Acts 8 — the evangelist who baptized the Ethiopian — is another man, one of the seven; this Philip is the apostle from Bethsaida.)

verses.text: Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.
When Jesus then lifted up his eyes, and saw a great company come unto him, he saith unto Philip, Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?
Philip answered him, Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little.
Philip saith unto him, Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us.

people.name: Bartholomew
people.identity: An Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile

ownWords.text: Nathanael answered and saith unto him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel.

story: Bartholomew stands in every list of the twelve — in Matthew, Mark and Luke always near Philip (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14), and again in the upper room in Acts (Acts 1:13) — yet no word of a man called Bartholomew is recorded anywhere in Scripture. The church has long known him as Nathanael of Cana, the man Philip brought to Jesus in John 1: Bartholomew is a surname — son of Tolmai — and Nathanael the given name it would carry. That identification is the church's tradition, held for centuries, and it is as Nathanael that his story is told here.

Philip found Nathanael and told him the news — Jesus of Nazareth, the one Moses and the prophets wrote of. Nathanael's answer was the honest skeptic's question: 'Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?' Philip did not argue the point; he said, 'Come and see' (John 1:46). Jesus saw him coming and said of him, 'Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!' — and when Nathanael asked how Jesus knew him, the answer undid him: 'Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee' (John 1:47–48).

Nathanael's confession is one of the first and fullest in all the Gospels: 'Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel' (John 1:49). Jesus promised the guileless man greater things than a fig tree — heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man (John 1:51). Nathanael is named again at the end, standing with the disciples by the sea of Tiberias when the risen Jesus showed himself to them (John 21:2) — still there, from the fig tree to the empty tomb to the upper room.

verses.text: And Nathanael said unto him, Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him, Come and see.
Nathanael answered and saith unto him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel.
There were together Simon Peter, and Thomas called Didymus, and Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two other of his disciples.
